newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Japan MOF still studying DKB punishment.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Japan MOF still studying DKB punishment.

text.p: The Finance Ministry will consider the impact on depositors and borrowers when deciding how to punish Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) for its involvement in a racketeer payoff scandal, a senior ministry official said on Thursday.

Sei Nakai, deputy director-general of the ministry's banking bureau, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) that the ministry would have to wait for further progress in prosecutors' investigation of the scandal before deciding on administrative penalties based on Japan's Banking Law.

But he added, "banks are a key part of the economic system and comprise the settlement system, and measures could have a great impact on depositors and small- and medium-sized firms which are borrowers, so we are studying what kind of measures are possible."

The "sokaiya" racketeer scandal has already led to the arrest of more than one dozen officials from DKB and Nomura Securities Co Ltd and DKB has acknowledged that it hid some of its dubious loans to the racketeer at the heart of the scandal from regular inspections by the finance ministry.

Asked whether penalties might include restrictions on DKB's foreign exchange business, Nakai said authorities would also have to take into account any impact on customers doing business with the bank.

Commenting on criticism that the current penalty under the Banking Law for submitting false reports is a maximum of 500,000 yen, Nakai said the ministry aimed to submit legal changes to increase the fine in an extra session of parliament expected to be held this autumn.

"The basic premise of the current law was that banks wouldn't do much wrong and it respected banks' autonomy, but unfortunately such an incident occurred and there has been debate over whether it (the penalty) is sufficient," he said.

Nakai said that a consensus was building among both members of parliament and ministry officials that 500,000 yen was too low a fine, but that no conclusion had yet been reached on how much it should be increased.

Commenting on a restructuring plan by Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB), which includes the bank's issuance of 386.40 million preferred shares worth 123.65 billion yen, Nakai said the plan was proceeding according to its original schedule.

NCB said on Monday the price of each share would be 320 yen and the payment date is July 28. A special fund set up by the Japanese government will purchase 250 million of the preferred shares, making it the largest buyer of shares.
"With regard to capital, there is not much concern," Nakai said, adding that the capital increase would result in NCB's having a capital-asset ratio of six percent.

From here on, much will depend on NCB's own strategic management efforts, Nakai said. "The (NCB) tie-up with Bankers Trust is one sign of that (strategy)," he said. "After dealing with its problem loans, NCB will be a slimmer bank, but we expect that it will be getting closer to being a healthy bank," he added.

Asked about prospects for the growth of a market for securitised assets, Nakai said foreign banks and brokers would increasingly provide technical expertise on the supply side. But he added that there was concern that Japanese investors were lagging behind their U.S. and European counterparts in their demand for high-risk, high-return investment products.

Britain's Barclays Bank recently announced it would discuss cooperation in several areas with Japan's troubled Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, including the development of new financial products and the securitisation of Hokkaido Takushoku's assets.
The tie-up followed an announcement of a similar alliance between NCB and Bankers Trust New York Corp.
